newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Suits or truce for tobacco makers in 1997?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Suits or truce for tobacco makers in 1997?.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent

The once-invincible U.S. tobacco industry, which found in 1996 that its seemingly bottomless legal war chest no longer scared off foes, enters 1997 facing a flood of lawsuits and speculation that a settlement is the only answer.

Litigation against cigarette companies has reached an all-time high, with hundreds of individual and class action personal injury suits filed across the country, 18 states suing to recoup health care costs of smokers and the Justice Department investigating allegations that manufacturers lied to federal agencies.

While the tobacco industry has won most of the personal injury cases brought over the past 40 years because juries held individuals responsible for their decision to keep smoking, many legal and financial experts think this attitude is changing.

A $750,000 Florida verdict against Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp in August is an indication that jurors have been angered by internal tobacco industry memos about the addictive nature of nicotine that have become public, and will increasingly find cigarette companies liable for smokers' illnesses, these experts say.

"Jurors no longer see this as a matter of choice...the fact this jury (in Florida) has sent a message to the world that they are willing to hold tobacco companies liable is a dramatic and significant result. It's not a fluke. It's not an aberration," said jury consultant Robert Gordon, director of the Dallas-based Wilmington Institute.
RISK OF LOSING CASES

Tobacco companies will most likely continue to win some and maybe even many of the suits but experts say they run a risk of losing big damaging cases that would send share prices plummeting and continue to boost their already soaring legal fees.

Mary Aronson, a Washington, D.C.-based institutional investment adviser, said she thought the industry should seriously consider negotiating a deal to indemnify itself against smokers' lawsuits before it suffers a big loss.
"I think they would be foolish to wait until then (losing a case)," Aronson said. "If the plaintiffs bar starts winning cases, they will be much harder to buy off."
She predicted an accord would boost share prices.
"That kind of vulnerability may be good for the industry," Aronson said of the Florida verdict. "It will force them to consider some sort of deal."

Some state attorneys general and plaintiffs lawyers are trying to come up with a legislative solution, but many believe reaching an accord that would satisfy all parties will be a lengthy and complex task if it is possible at all.

"I expect some movement on this in the next congressional session. I can't tell you exactly what form it will take but I expect some movement and I expect to be involved," said Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, who has been pushing for a settlement.
FINAL SETTLEMENT COULD TAKE TIME

Moore cautioned that a final settlement could take some time, if one is reached at all, and was unlikely before three state lawsuits against the industry go to trial in 1997. He said talks aimed at a settlement have been escalating but his group has not yet directly met tobacco officials and continues to work through intermediaries.

"We've been meeting about it a lot. I'm real optimistic," he said. He pointed to remarks by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp Chief Executive Officer Steven Goldstone as possible evidence that top ranking executives would consider an accord.

In a December 5 speech to executives in Boston, Goldstone said many forces were at work favouring a settlement with the tobacco industry. "In 1997, the most meaningful thing I can do is come to some solution on this problem," he added.

Daniel Donahue, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. senior vice president and deputy general counsel managing the tobacco litigation, denied that his company was in any settlement talks and said it planned to keep fighting the suits.

"We are not in the process of any kind of negotiations or discussions of any kind of settlement, primarily because these attempts by plaintiffs lawyers to twist and turn the litigation system of this country are basically wrong," he said, adding that he expected to "successfully defend" the cases.
The new year will certainly provide plenty of opportunities for the industry to show if it can maintain a winning streak.

As early as February 10, the industry will argue against Food and Drug Administration plans to limit cigarette advertising and marketing. Suits by Mississippi, Florida and Texas seeking to recoup the costs of health care for poor smokers are scheduled for trial in 1997 along with at least two of the class actions.
